topic: Rejecting the model made the decision defence
stem: A team argues that because a wrong output was generated by the model rather than by any person, the organisation is not answerable for the resulting harm. What is the correct principle?

options.text: The organisation deployed the system and acted on its output, so the outcome is the organisation's whichever component produced it.
Accountability is shared with the model provider in proportion to the provider's contribution to the error, as established by the incident investigation.
The organisation is answerable only where it can be shown to have departed from the provider's documented guidance for using the model.
Accountability rests with the individual who authored the prompt, since that is the instruction that shaped the output in question.

explanation.correct: Deploying a system is a decision, and so is acting on what it produces. The organisation chose the use case, chose to automate it, chose what oversight to place around it, and chose to release the output into the world. Every one of those is a human decision that a customer, a court or a supervisor can examine. Distributing blame onto a component is not a position the organisation can adopt externally, and internally it removes the incentive to build the oversight that would have caught the error.

distractors.B: Contract may allocate cost between the parties, but it does not divide answerability to the affected person. The provider had no visibility of the use case, the data, or the decision the output fed, and the person harmed dealt only with the deploying organisation.
distractors.C: Following supplier guidance is evidence of care, not a defence. Guidance is written for general use and cannot anticipate a specific deployment; the deploying organisation still had to decide whether the system was fit for its own purpose.
distractors.D: Blaming the prompt author personalises a systemic failure. The prompt was written inside a process the organisation designed, reviewed and approved, and treating the author as the responsible party guarantees the next author hides problems rather than raising them.

explanation.concept: Accountability for an AI outcome follows the decision to deploy and to act, not the mechanism that produced the output. A model is a component; components do not bear responsibility. Neither the provider nor an individual contributor absorbs the organisation's answerability for its own use.
explanation.tip: Any answer that moves accountability off the deploying organisation — onto a model, a supplier, or one engineer — is wrong in this domain. The only question is which human inside the organisation holds it.

topic: Acceptable-use policy that does not reach contract staff
stem: A Swedish architecture practice issues its AI acceptable-use policy through the employee handbook, acknowledged at onboarding. About a third of production work on a large hospital project is delivered by freelance draughtspeople engaged through an agency, working on their own laptops with access to the practice's cloud file share. A reviewer finds AI-generated specification text in a deliverable produced by one of them, describing a fire-rating standard that does not exist. What is the governing weakness?

options.text: The practice has no reliable way to detect AI-generated text, so it should apply a detection tool to every incoming deliverable before it is accepted into the project record.
The freelancers work on their own laptops and are outside endpoint monitoring, so the practice should require practice-issued devices for all contract staff before granting file share access.
The policy is bound to the employment relationship and does not reach the people producing a third of the work; the obligation has to sit in the engagement contract and the agency's terms.
The specification text should have been caught in the practice's design review, so the remedy is to add an AI-content question to the existing review checklist and brief reviewers on it.

explanation.correct: A policy delivered through an employee handbook and acknowledged at onboarding binds employees. The people who produced this deliverable are not employees, never saw the handbook, and have no contractual obligation to follow it — so the practice has no enforceable requirement covering a third of its output on this project. Fixing the detection or the review catches individual instances after the fact; fixing the instrument means flowing the obligation into the engagement contracts and the agency's terms, where it can actually be required, evidenced and enforced.

distractors.A: Detection tooling for machine-generated text is unreliable in both directions and would produce disputes with contractors who are under no obligation in the first place. It also treats every deliverable as suspect rather than establishing the standard people are working to.
distractors.B: Device control narrows one channel and creates a substantial cost and friction for short-term contract staff. It does nothing about what those staff are permitted to do on a practice-issued laptop, which is a policy question the practice has still not answered for them.
distractors.D: Strengthening design review is worth doing and would have caught this specification. It is a detective control at the end of the process, and it leaves the practice relying on reviewers to find every instance rather than on contributors being bound not to create them.

explanation.concept: An AI acceptable-use policy reaches only as far as the instrument that carries it. Employees are bound by employment terms; contractors, agency staff and outsourced teams are bound only by what is written into their engagement contracts. Map the policy against every population that touches your work product.
explanation.tip: When a stem tells you what proportion of the work is done by non-employees and how the policy was issued, it is pointing at coverage, not at detection.

topic: Rebuilding an incident severity matrix for AI failures
stem: A Vietnamese digital bank is extending its incident severity matrix to cover AI failures. The current matrix rates severity on number of users affected and duration of the outage. Applied to recent events, it rated an AI failure that produced incorrect but entirely plausible tax statements for twelve customers at the lowest severity, while a forty-minute degradation of an internal dashboard rated two levels higher. Which set of dimensions should the AI severity rating be built on?

options.text: Number of affected users, outage duration and the model tier in use, so that AI severity stays comparable with the existing matrix and can be applied by the same triage team without retraining.
Whether the output reached a person or drove an action, how severe and reversible the consequence is, and whether an oversight step should have caught it.
Financial exposure estimated at the moment of declaration, so that AI incidents can be prioritised against the bank's other operational risk events on a single monetary scale.
Confidence scores logged by the system when the failure occurred, so that severity reflects how far the model's behaviour departed from its expected operating range at the time.

explanation.correct: The mis-rating happened because the existing dimensions measure the wrong thing: availability failures scale with users and minutes, but AI failures scale with what the wrong output caused. Twelve plausible-looking incorrect tax statements is a small number of users and no downtime at all, yet each one is an authoritative document a customer may act on and that may be hard to unwind. Reach, severity and reversibility of the consequence, and whether an oversight step failed, capture exactly what the availability dimensions cannot — and the oversight dimension also tells you whether the control environment or only the model is at fault.

distractors.A: Retaining users and duration preserves the defect the bank has just observed, and adding model tier makes it worse: a cheap model producing a wrong tax statement is more serious than a capable model producing a wrong internal summary, so the dimension points the wrong way.
distractors.C: A single monetary scale is attractive for prioritisation and useless at declaration time, because the financial exposure of twelve incorrect statements is unknown for weeks. Severity has to be assignable in minutes from facts the responder actually has.
distractors.D: Model confidence signals are unreliable, are not comparable across tasks, and are frequently highest on exactly the plausible-but-wrong outputs that cause the most harm. Severity is about consequence in the world, not about the system's internal state.

explanation.concept: AI incident severity is a function of reach, consequence severity and reversibility, and whether an oversight step failed — not of availability. Rate on what the wrong output caused, using facts a responder can establish within minutes of declaration.
explanation.tip: When a stem contrasts a low-user, no-downtime AI failure that rated low with a trivial outage that rated high, the matrix's dimensions are the finding. Look for the option that swaps availability for consequence.

topic: Distinguishing Consulted from Informed in an AI approval RACI
stem: In a RACI covering approval of a new AI use case, what distinguishes a Consulted party from an Informed one?

options.text: A Consulted party can veto the decision outright; an Informed party can only have an objection recorded in the minutes.
A Consulted party attends the approval meeting in person; an Informed party receives the papers in advance and may submit comments.
A Consulted party is drawn from the second line of defence, while an Informed party is drawn from the first line.
A Consulted party's input must be sought and addressed before the decision is taken; an Informed party is told once it has been.

explanation.correct: The distinction is about timing and obligation, not seniority or attendance. Consulted creates a duty on the decision-maker: their view must be actively sought and the decision record must show it was considered, so a decision taken without consulting them is procedurally defective. Informed creates a duty only to communicate afterwards. This matters in AI approvals because functions such as data protection or the affected business area are frequently listed as Informed when the organisation actually needs their input to bind the decision.

distractors.A: Veto power is a decision right, which in RACI terms would make the party Accountable or a joint decision-maker. Consulted parties can object strongly and force escalation, but the decision remains with the accountable owner.
distractors.B: Attendance is a mechanism for consultation, not its definition. A Consulted party can be consulted in writing without attending anything, and attendance without any obligation to address the input is exactly the pattern that hollows out approval boards.
distractors.C: RACI roles describe involvement in a specific decision and map onto no particular line of defence. First-line business owners are routinely Consulted, and second-line functions are sometimes only Informed for low-tier use cases.

explanation.concept: Consulted means two-way and before; Informed means one-way and after. When designing an AI approval RACI, place any function whose objection would change the decision in Consulted, and require the decision record to show how their input was addressed.
explanation.tip: RACI recall items usually turn on before-versus-after and duty-versus-courtesy. Options phrased in terms of seniority, attendance or organisational line are distractors.

topic: Finding developer shadow AI that leaves no spend trail
stem: A Scottish renewables developer ran a shadow AI sweep across corporate card spend, expense claims and vendor invoices, and found nothing beyond the two registered platforms. A subsequent code review turned up model API calls in three internal repositories, authenticated with keys that do not map to any corporate billing account. Two of the three run in production against turbine maintenance records. Which TWO detection methods would have found this use? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Scanning source repositories and CI configuration for model provider SDK imports, API endpoint hostnames and credential patterns.
Reviewing corporate card statements and vendor invoices again at a lower value threshold than the sweep used, to catch small or trial-tier charges.
Inspecting egress from build agents and production workloads for outbound connections to model provider API hostnames.
Requiring engineering managers to attest each quarter that none of their teams calls an unapproved model API from any repository they own.
Auditing single sign-on application consents to identify AI products that have been connected to the corporate identity tenant.

explanation.correct: The stem rules out the money trail explicitly: the keys map to no corporate billing account, so no threshold on card or invoice data will surface them. What is left is the code and the traffic. Repository and pipeline scanning finds the integration at rest — the import, the hostname, the credential pattern — and covers code that is written but not yet deployed. Egress inspection from build agents and production workloads finds it in motion, and catches integrations that scanning misses because they were configured rather than coded. Together they cover both the artefact and the behaviour.

distractors.B: Rerunning the financial sweep at a finer threshold searches a data set the stem has already told you does not contain the answer. Personal or free-tier credentials generate no corporate charge at any value.
distractors.D: Manager attestation is self-report with an extra layer, and the managers concerned may genuinely not know what is in every repository their teams own. It also asks people to declare something that may reflect badly on them.
distractors.E: Identity consent auditing is a strong technique for finding software-as-a-service AI products connected to corporate data, which is a different failure mode. Direct API calls with a developer's own key never touch the identity tenant.

explanation.concept: Different shadow AI populations leave different traces. Business users leave spend and identity consents; developers leave code, pipeline configuration and egress. A discovery programme that covers only one class of signal will report a clean estate while another class runs unregistered.
explanation.tip: Read the stem for which signal has already been excluded. Once it says the keys carry no corporate billing, every finance-based option is dead regardless of how it is refined.

topic: Conditional AI approval recorded as unconditional
stem: A Peruvian mining company's AI board approved a geotechnical-risk summarisation assistant subject to three conditions: an evaluation set covering five years of incident reports, a documented escalation route to a qualified geotechnical engineer, and a post-implementation review at six months. The assistant went live nine months ago. None of the three conditions has been evidenced, no record shows anyone tracking them, and the approval register displays the status 'Approved'. What does this indicate, and what should be fixed?

options.text: Conditional approval is being recorded as unconditional: conditions need owners, dates and a closure gate, and the status should read as approved with open conditions until each is evidenced.
The board attached too many conditions to a single decision and should instead defer approval entirely until the requesting team has already satisfied every condition it intends to impose.
The missing control is the post-implementation review; had it been scheduled at the point of approval, it would have surfaced the two outstanding conditions within the intended six months.
The three conditions were operational rather than governance matters, and should have been raised as delivery requirements with the project manager rather than attached to a board approval.

explanation.correct: The board decided that the assistant was acceptable only with those three things in place, and the register now says it is acceptable full stop. Anyone reading the register — an auditor, a new owner, the board itself — sees an approved system, and the conditions have no existence outside the minutes of one meeting. This is a system that is running with an unrepresentative evaluation set, no documented route to a qualified engineer, and no review, in a domain where a missed geotechnical risk is a safety matter. The fix is structural: conditions become tracked items with owners and dates, and the approval status carries their state.

distractors.B: Requiring every condition to be met before approval removes a useful mechanism. Some conditions can only be satisfied after deployment, such as a post-implementation review, and forcing full pre-satisfaction pushes teams to argue conditions away rather than accept them.
distractors.C: The review is one of the three unclosed conditions, so treating it as the missing control assumes the very tracking that is absent. Scheduling it would have depended on somebody owning it, which is the gap being described.
distractors.D: An evaluation set representative of the risk domain and an escalation route to a qualified engineer are the conditions on which the risk decision rested. Reclassifying them as delivery detail removes them from the board's oversight entirely.

explanation.concept: A conditional approval is only a control if the conditions are tracked like any other commitment: named owner, due date, evidence of closure, and an approval status that reflects whether they are open. Otherwise the conditions are advice and the approval is unconditional in practice.
explanation.tip: Whenever a stem quotes conditions attached to an approval, check whether anything in the process would ever notice them again. If the answer is nothing, that is the item.

topic: What the blameless convention buys a postmortem
stem: AI incident postmortems are conducted blamelessly — describing what people did and why it made sense to them at the time, without attributing fault. What does that convention buy the organisation?

options.text: It keeps the postmortem document suitable for sharing with external auditors and reviewers without further redaction.
It guarantees that no individual faces any consequence for an error, which is what makes staff willing to take part at all.
It produces a fuller and more accurate account, by removing the incentive to leave detail out.
It shortens the time needed to produce the postmortem, by avoiding arguments about who was responsible for what.

explanation.correct: A postmortem is only as good as what people are willing to say. When the document determines who gets blamed, participants edit — they omit the workaround they used, the alert they silenced, the shortcut everyone takes. Those omissions are usually the most informative facts available, because they describe the real system rather than the designed one. Removing fault attribution changes the calculation and gets the full sequence on the page, which is the only basis on which useful preventive actions can be identified.

distractors.A: External shareability is a convenient side effect at best. Blameless postmortems are often more candid about internal weaknesses than a document written for outside readers would be, so publication usually still requires judgement.
distractors.B: Blameless does not mean consequence-free. Deliberate misconduct or repeated disregard for a control is still handled through the appropriate route; what the convention removes is fault-finding as the purpose of the technical investigation.
distractors.D: Speed is not the point and blameless reviews are frequently slower, because they push further into contributing conditions rather than stopping at the first person who made a mistake.

explanation.concept: Blameless postmortems are an information-gathering technique, not a kindness. The organisation trades the satisfaction of assigning fault for the accuracy of the account, because accurate accounts are what produce actions that stop recurrence.
explanation.tip: Ask what the convention is for rather than what it feels like. Options framed around protecting individuals or producing shareable documents describe effects, not purpose.

topic: Controlling incident communications across three teams
stem: A Greek shipping line's Claude-based cargo documentation assistant produced incorrect dangerous-goods classifications on shipping documents for two days. The incident was declared thirty minutes ago and the assistant is disabled. Operations, compliance and IT are each contacting customers, port agents and the classification society separately, and two of them have already given different figures for how many shipments are affected. Port agents need corrected classifications before the next vessel sails at 18:00. What should the incident lead do next?

options.text: Ask all three teams to pause outbound communication until the affected shipment count is confirmed, then issue a single agreed statement to every audience at once.
Establish a single source of truth for incident facts and a named communications owner, and require every outbound message to be drawn from it.
Escalate to the executive sponsor so that a decision can be taken on whether the classification society must be notified formally.
Move compliance and IT onto the technical investigation and leave operations to handle all external communication on its own.

explanation.correct: Two constraints are pulling against each other: the messages must stop contradicting one another, and corrected classifications must reach port agents before 18:00. A fact base plus a named communications owner satisfies both — communication continues, but everyone draws from the same numbers, and one person is answerable for what goes out. It also fixes the underlying cause, which is that three teams are each maintaining their own private view of the incident. This is the standard incident-command separation of the technical response from the communications response.

distractors.A: A communications freeze resolves the inconsistency by stopping the flow, which is not available here. Port agents need corrected dangerous-goods classifications before the vessel sails, and holding them for a confirmed count trades an accuracy problem for a safety one.
distractors.C: Notifying the classification society is very likely necessary and is a decision for the accountable executive, but it addresses one audience while three teams continue to contradict each other across all of them. It is a parallel action, not the next one.
distractors.D: Reducing the number of communicators to one team helps consistency and loses the specialist knowledge each audience needs. Operations cannot speak to a classification society on technical grounds, and the underlying problem — no shared fact base — would persist.

explanation.concept: Incident communications need a single fact base and one named owner, distinct from the technical response lead. Consistency comes from everyone drawing on the same source, not from silencing the channels — particularly when an audience needs information urgently for safety reasons.
explanation.tip: Watch for a hard external deadline in the stem. It is usually there to eliminate the option that pauses everything until the picture is complete.

topic: Authorising reuse of an internal data set for an AI build
stem: A Malaysian telco's care team is building a Claude assistant and wants to use ten years of contact-centre transcripts as few-shot examples and as its evaluation set. The transcripts sit in a system owned by the customer operations directorate; the AI team obtained a copy informally from a data-engineering colleague. The telco's governance standard requires that reuse of a data set for a purpose other than the one it was collected for be authorised by that data set's owner. The AI team's position is that the data never leaves the company. What is the governance defect?

options.text: The transcripts contain customer identifiers and ought to be de-identified before any use in prompts or evaluation, and the absence of that step is the defect the standard exists to catch.
Few-shot examples and evaluation cases must be drawn from disjoint samples, and using the same ten-year corpus for both will contaminate the evaluation and overstate measured quality.
Ten years of transcripts far exceeds what the use case needs, and the team should have requested a smaller and more recent sample proportionate to the task it is supporting.
The data is being used for a purpose other than the one it was collected for, and only the owner can authorise that change; the informal transfer bypassed the decision entirely.

explanation.correct: The standard quoted in the stem turns on purpose and on who decides, and both were skipped. Transcripts captured for service quality and dispute handling are now being used to shape and measure a product, which is a different purpose, and the person with the standing to weigh that — the customer operations director who owns the data set and its commitments to customers — was never asked. The argument that the data stays inside the company answers a question about disclosure that the standard is not asking. Internal transfers between directorates are precisely what the authorisation requirement governs.

distractors.A: De-identification is very likely a condition the data owner would attach, and it may be required on other grounds. It is a control the owner would impose as part of authorising the use, so proposing it as the defect assumes the authorisation step that never happened.
distractors.B: Overlap between few-shot examples and evaluation cases is a genuine methodological error that would inflate the measured results, but it is an evaluation design problem. It says nothing about whether the team was entitled to hold the corpus at all.
distractors.C: Taking more data than the task requires is poor practice and would be worth challenging. Proportionality is about how much of an authorised data set to use; here the issue is that no authorisation exists for any quantity.

explanation.concept: Internal data reuse is a governance decision with a named decider: the data owner. 'It never left the company' addresses disclosure, not purpose. Any AI build that draws on an existing operational data set needs the owner's authorisation recorded before the data is copied.
explanation.tip: When a stem quotes an internal standard, resolve the item against its exact wording. Here 'purpose other than the one it was collected for' and 'authorised by the owner' decide it, and the technically sound-sounding options are all about something else.

topic: Making a board AI risk appetite statement operable
stem: What makes a board-level AI risk appetite statement operable rather than decorative?

options.text: It states limits an approval body can apply to a specific proposal — which categories of decision may be automated, and what must always retain human sign-off.
It is reviewed and reaffirmed by the board annually, with the review recorded in the minutes and reported onward to the audit committee for assurance.
It is expressed in the same language and on the same scale as the organisation's other risk appetite statements, so that AI risk can be aggregated with them.
It is communicated to every member of staff through the AI usage policy, so that everyone understands the level of risk the organisation is prepared to accept.

explanation.correct: A risk appetite statement earns its place only if someone downstream can use it to decide a case. The test is whether an approval body, holding a specific proposal, can read the statement and determine whether the proposal is inside or outside appetite. That requires content of the form 'these categories of decision may be automated; these require human sign-off in every case; these are not undertaken at all'. A statement that expresses a general attitude to innovation cannot resolve any proposal, so approvals fall back on the judgement of whoever is in the room.

distractors.B: Annual reaffirmation keeps the statement current and evidences board engagement. It does nothing about whether the content can be applied to a decision, and a vague statement reaffirmed every year is vague for another year.
distractors.C: Consistency of scale and language supports aggregation and reporting, and it is a reasonable thing to want. Aggregating an unusable statement produces a comparable number that still cannot decide whether a specific proposal should proceed.
distractors.D: Broad communication is useful for awareness. Appetite statements are addressed to decision-makers rather than to all staff, and the decision that matters is made at the approval gate, not by individuals reading the policy.

explanation.concept: Test any risk appetite statement by handing it to an approval body with a live proposal. If the body cannot use it to say yes or no, it is a values statement. Operable appetite names categories of decision, required oversight, and prohibited uses.
explanation.tip: Prefer the option that lets someone decide a specific case. Governance artefacts that only get reviewed, aggregated or communicated are being described by their process, not by their use.

topic: Why training completion is a weak governance metric
stem: An organisation reports 'percentage of staff who completed AI policy training' as its primary AI governance metric. Why is that a weak choice?

options.text: It is a lagging indicator, and governance metrics should be leading indicators that predict where the next control failure will occur.
It measures an input the organisation controls completely, and will read close to full compliance whether or not any prohibited use has actually stopped.
It cannot be benchmarked against comparable organisations, so the board is given a figure with no external reference against which to judge whether it is good or bad.
It excludes contractors and agency staff, and until they are brought into scope the figure cannot properly be reported to the board at all.

explanation.correct: The organisation sets the deadline, sends the reminders, and can make completion a condition of system access, so the number converges on full compliance by construction. It therefore carries almost no information: a quarter in which shadow AI doubled and a quarter in which it fell to nothing produce the same figure. A useful governance metric moves when the control environment changes — registered proportion of the estate, exceptions open past expiry, mean time to declare an AI incident, blocked policy violations at the gateway. Completion measures effort expended, not risk reduced.

distractors.A: Training completion is actually a leading measure in the conventional sense, since it precedes the behaviour it hopes to influence. The problem is not where it sits on the leading–lagging axis but that it is insensitive to the outcome it is standing in for.
distractors.C: External benchmarking is nice to have and rarely decisive for internal control metrics. A metric that is unbenchmarkable but responsive to the control environment is far more useful than a comparable one that never moves.
distractors.D: Coverage gaps are a real weakness in many training populations and worth fixing. Extending the metric to contractors would produce a broader figure with exactly the same defect: it would still sit near full compliance regardless of behaviour.

explanation.concept: Choose governance metrics that can get worse. If a measure will read near-perfect whatever happens to the underlying risk, it provides assurance without evidence. Prefer coverage of the estate, exception ageing, time to detect and declare, and violations actually prevented.
explanation.tip: Ask what value the metric would take in a bad quarter. If the answer is the same as in a good one, it is not a control metric.

topic: Bringing an acquired company's AI estate under governance
stem: A Turkish conglomerate has acquired a 200-person insurtech. Due diligence covered financials, intellectual property and security, but not AI. On the first day of integration the acquirer finds four customer-facing AI features in production, none of them registered anywhere, one of which generates pricing recommendations that underwriters accept without change in most cases. The group standard requires all AI in the group to be registered and risk-tiered within ninety days of acquisition, and it reserves suspension of a live feature to the approval board on evidence of harm or of a breached obligation. No such evidence has emerged: the target reports no complaints, no loss events and no regulator contact on any of the four. Which TWO actions should be prioritised inside that window? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Register all four as use cases with a named accountable owner drawn from the group's structure, and tier them on consequence and autonomy.
Migrate all four features onto the acquirer's model gateway before the ninety days expire, so that they fall under central logging and credential control immediately.
Establish what the target's customer contracts and its own AI vendor contracts say about model data use, since those terms transferred with the business and now bind the group.
Suspend the pricing-recommendation feature until the acquirer's approval board has reviewed it, on the grounds that it affects customers and has never been assessed.
Require every engineer at the target to complete the group's AI policy training and sign the acceptable-use attestation within the first month of integration.

explanation.correct: The ninety-day requirement is registration and tiering, and that is achievable: it needs discovery, owners and a risk assessment, not re-engineering. Assigning owners from the group structure is the part that matters most, because the target's own owners may not survive integration and the pricing feature currently has nobody in the acquirer answerable for it. The second priority is contractual, and it is time-sensitive in a way that is easy to miss: the target's obligations to its customers and the terms it agreed with its own AI suppliers transferred at completion, so the group is already bound by commitments it has not read.

distractors.B: Gateway migration is the right destination and the wrong first move. Re-platforming four production features in ninety days competes directly with the registration work the standard actually requires, and it cannot begin sensibly until the features are understood and owned.
distractors.D: The standard reserves suspension to the approval board on evidence of harm or of a breached obligation, and the stem states there is none, so this is not an action the integration team can prioritise. It also inverts the sequence: assess the pricing feature urgently at a high tier, and let suspension be an outcome the assessment might reach rather than a starting position.
distractors.E: Training and attestation give the group a paper record and change nothing about four unregistered production systems. It is also the least time-critical item in the list, since the target's engineers are not the source of the exposure.

explanation.concept: Post-acquisition AI integration starts with registration, ownership and tiering, plus a read of the contractual commitments that transferred with the business. Technical consolidation and awareness activity follow, because neither reduces exposure while the estate is still unowned and undescribed.
explanation.tip: In multi-select prioritisation items, anchor on the requirement the stem states — here, registration and tiering in ninety days. Options that are valuable but do not serve that requirement are the distractors.

topic: A route for staff to raise concerns about a live AI system
stem: An analyst at an Italian energy retailer believes the Claude-based retention-offer assistant is systematically offering worse terms to customers in certain postcodes. She raised it with her line manager, who replied that the model receives no postcode input and closed the conversation. Six weeks later nothing has been logged anywhere, and the assistant continues to run. What does the governance framework most need here?

options.text: Commission an evaluation of the assistant's outputs segmented by postcode, so the analyst's claim can be tested against data rather than argued from what inputs the model receives.
Introduce a rule that any concern about model fairness is escalated to the second line of defence for determination rather than being resolved by the employee's own line manager.
A route by which any employee can log an AI concern directly into the governance record, where it is triaged and closed with a recorded outcome, whatever their manager's view.
Make bias testing mandatory at approval time for every customer-facing AI system, so that concerns of this kind are identified and dealt with before the system reaches production.

explanation.correct: Two failures compound here. One person with no stake in the outcome was able to end the inquiry, and there is no record that it ever happened — so nobody reviewing this system will learn that a concern was raised, and the analyst has no way to know whether anything was done. A direct logging route fixes both: the concern enters the governance record independently of the manager's judgement, it gets triaged by people who can commission testing, and it closes with a documented outcome. Note also that the manager's reasoning is unsound, since a model can produce postcode-correlated outcomes from correlated inputs without ever seeing a postcode.

distractors.A: The segmented evaluation is very likely the right investigation and may well be what triage commissions. It answers this specific concern while leaving the next one to depend on whether the employee's manager happens to take it seriously.
distractors.B: Routing fairness concerns to the second line is narrower than the problem and still leaves the manager as the gate. It also carves out one category, so a concern about hallucinated safety guidance would meet the same dead end.
distractors.D: Pre-deployment bias testing is sound practice and should be in place. It cannot address behaviour observed in production against real customers months after approval, which is exactly the situation the analyst is describing.

explanation.concept: Provide a channel that lets any employee put a concern about a live AI system into the governance record directly, with triage and a recorded outcome. Concerns that can be closed verbally by one manager leave no trace, and the absence of logged concerns then reads as an absence of problems.
explanation.tip: When a stem says nothing was logged, the gap is the channel, not the investigation. Ask what would happen to the next person who noticed something.

topic: Extending an approved AI system to a new group entity
stem: A Colombian retail group has an approved Claude-based complaint triage assistant running in its home market. It now wants to run the identical system — same code, same prompts, same model, same hosting — for a recently acquired Ecuadorian subsidiary. The group standard requires re-approval wherever the risk profile changes materially. Which TWO things must be assessed before the extension proceeds? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Whether the evaluation set represents the subsidiary's complaint mix, product range and language use, since the recorded performance was measured entirely on home-market cases.
Whether the underlying model performs equivalently at the higher request volume, since combined traffic across both markets will roughly double.
Who the accountable owner is in the subsidiary, and whether the escalation route to a human complaint handler exists and is staffed there.
Whether the subsidiary's staff have completed the group's AI policy training before the assistant is made available to them.
Whether the system should be rebuilt on the subsidiary's own infrastructure so that the two markets do not share a technical dependency.

explanation.correct: Nothing about the system is changing, which is exactly why the extension looks safe and is not. The evidence supporting the original approval was gathered on one market's complaints, and performance on cases the evaluation set never contained is unknown — different products, different complaint patterns, different phrasing. Separately, the oversight arrangement the approval assumed is a property of the home market, not of the code: the escalation route to a human handler has to exist and be staffed in the subsidiary, and somebody in that entity has to be accountable for the system's behaviour there.

distractors.B: Doubling volume is a capacity and cost question. It may need rate limit and concurrency work, but the risk per decision is unchanged, and the group standard is concerned with risk profile rather than throughput.
distractors.D: Policy training is a general obligation for staff in a group entity rather than a condition specific to this extension. It gives the group an awareness record and tells it nothing about whether the assistant works on Ecuadorian complaints.
distractors.E: Where the system runs is an architecture decision that could be argued either way, and shared infrastructure is often the more controlled option. It has no bearing on whether the system behaves correctly for a new population.

explanation.concept: Extending an approved AI system to a new population or entity is a new risk decision even when the system is byte-identical. Approval rests on evaluation evidence gathered on a specific population and on an oversight arrangement that lives in a specific organisation; neither travels with the code.
explanation.tip: 'Same code, same prompts, same model' in a stem is the trap. It invites you to conclude nothing changed, when the population and the oversight arrangement both did.

topic: Stating permitted use rather than only prohibited use
stem: Why should an AI usage policy state what is permitted rather than only listing what is prohibited?

options.text: A permitted-use statement gives staff a decidable answer for the cases the prohibition list does not name, which is most of them.
Prohibition lists cannot be enforced without a disciplinary framework, whereas a permitted-use statement enforces itself through the sanctioned platform.
A permitted-use statement removes the need to maintain a list of named tools, because permissions can be written against categories of use instead.
Prohibition lists must be reviewed far more frequently than permission lists, because new AI products appear continuously and each one requires assessment.

explanation.correct: A prohibition list is finite and the space of possible uses is not, so a policy built only from prohibitions leaves an employee with a novel case and no way to resolve it. Under time pressure the usual resolution is to assume that anything not forbidden is allowed. Stating what is permitted — which categories of work, on which data classifications, through which platforms — makes the default answer 'not yet approved, here is how to ask', which is both decidable at the desk and a route into the governance process rather than around it.

distractors.B: Neither form of statement enforces itself. Enforcement comes from a chokepoint that inspects or blocks, and a permitted-use statement without a gateway behind it is just as dependent on people choosing to comply as a prohibition is.
distractors.C: Permission statements can be written against categories, and so can prohibitions. Category-based drafting is a style choice available to both, and most organisations still end up maintaining a tool list for procurement and support reasons.
distractors.D: Both lists need regular review, and permission lists arguably need it more, since each new sanctioned tool has to be assessed before it can be added. Review frequency is not what distinguishes them.

explanation.concept: Write AI usage policy so that a member of staff facing an unlisted case reaches a defensible answer. Permitted-use framing makes the default 'ask' rather than 'assume allowed', and it channels novel cases into the approval process instead of into a gap in the prohibition list.
explanation.tip: Policy-drafting items reward whichever option changes what happens in the unlisted case. Enforcement mechanics and maintenance burden are separate concerns.

topic: Approved gateway credential used for an undeclared purpose
stem: A Japanese consumer electronics maker routes all Claude access through an internal gateway; each registered use case receives its own credential with a declared purpose recorded against it. A platform engineer reviewing gateway logs notices that the credential registered for supplier contract summarisation is also carrying prompts that classify the tone of employee performance review text. The team says it is a small experiment and that no decisions are being taken from the output. What is the correct response?

options.text: Treat the deviation as minor, record it in the log review notes, and ask the team to register the second use case when the next quarterly registration cycle opens.
Revoke the credential immediately, accepting that this also halts the approved contract-summarisation work until the team completes a fresh registration covering both uses.
Add employee performance content to the gateway's blocked patterns so that these prompts are rejected whichever credential submits them, without acting against the team.
Stop the unapproved use now and require it to be registered and assessed as its own use case with its own credential, since the declared purpose is the unit of approval.

explanation.correct: The whole design of this gateway rests on one credential meaning one assessed purpose — that is what makes the register reconcilable and what makes each entry's risk tier mean anything. A credential carrying two purposes silently invalidates both the register entry and the assessment behind it, and here the second purpose involves employee performance data, which almost certainly sits in a different risk tier from supplier contracts. The experimental framing does not change the analysis: unassessed processing of employee data is happening now, and 'no decisions are being taken' is an assertion nobody has verified and that can change without anyone being told.

distractors.A: Allowing an unassessed use of employee data to continue for up to a quarter treats the registration cycle as the constraint rather than the risk. It also establishes that using an existing credential for something new is tolerated if the team calls it an experiment.
distractors.B: Blanket revocation stops the violation and an approved business process along with it. Proportionality matters if the platform team wants business units to keep bringing work to the gateway rather than routing around it, and the approved use has done nothing wrong.
distractors.C: Content blocking addresses one data type and leaves the structural defect intact: credentials can still be reused for other undeclared purposes. It also fixes the symptom silently, so the register continues to describe an estate that does not exist.

explanation.concept: Where registration is enforced through per-use-case credentials, the declared purpose is the unit of approval and credential reuse is a governance breach rather than a technical shortcut. Stop the undeclared use, register it separately, and keep the approved use running.
explanation.tip: Look for the response that is both immediate and proportionate. Options that punish the compliant work alongside the violation, or that wait for the next cycle, are usually calibrated wrong in opposite directions.

topic: An AI risk forum with no decision rights
stem: A Philippine business process outsourcer runs a monthly AI risk forum whose terms of reference say it 'reviews and notes AI risks and escalates as appropriate'. Over the past year it noted forty risks; thirty-one remain open, and none was ever escalated, because 'as appropriate' was never defined and no member holds authority to halt or vary a client programme. What change would make the forum effective?

options.text: Appoint the chief risk officer as chair, so that the forum is led by someone senior enough for its views to carry weight with the client programme directors who would have to act on them.
Give the forum defined decision rights and a written escalation trigger — what it can require, what it must refer upward, and by when — so that noting a risk produces an owned, dated action.
Narrow the forum's scope to the highest-tier client programmes, so that the thirty-one open items reduce to a list the forum can realistically work through each month.
Move the forum to a fortnightly cadence so that open risks are revisited far more often and none can sit untouched for a full year before being discussed again.

explanation.correct: The terms of reference describe a body that observes. 'Notes' creates no obligation on anyone, and 'as appropriate' leaves escalation to a judgement nobody is required to make, which is why forty observations produced no actions in a year. Defining what the forum can require of a programme, what it must refer upward and within what period converts each noted risk into something with an owner and a date. Without decision rights the forum's output is commentary, and the volume of commentary is not the problem.

distractors.A: A senior chair can create influence, and influence sometimes substitutes for authority. It depends entirely on one individual's willingness to spend capital, produces inconsistent outcomes across programmes, and vanishes the moment that person changes role.
distractors.C: Reducing scope shrinks the list of things the forum fails to act on. The thirty-one open items are open because nothing obliges anyone to close them, and that is equally true of a shorter list.
distractors.D: More frequent meetings raise the rate at which risks are discussed and re-noted. Cadence changes throughput, not authority, and a fortnightly forum with no decision rights simply produces eighty observations instead of forty.

explanation.concept: A governance forum is defined by its decision rights. Specify what it can require, what it must escalate, to whom and within what period; otherwise it produces a register of noted risks that documents the organisation's awareness of problems it never addressed.
explanation.tip: Read the terms of reference quoted in the stem. Verbs like 'reviews', 'notes' and 'considers' with no obligation attached are the finding, and options about chairing, cadence or scope leave them untouched.

topic: Answering a board question the AI register cannot support
stem: Following press coverage of an AI failure at a competitor, an Argentine bank's board has asked the CEO to report at next month's meeting on which customer-facing decisions are made or influenced by an AI system, and who signs off each one. The bank's AI register holds system name, business unit, model and go-live date. It does not record whether a system is customer-facing, whether its output is acted on without human review, or who the accountable owner is. What should the chief risk officer do next?

options.text: Commission a full re-registration of the entire estate against a revised schema, and inform the board at next month's meeting that a complete answer will follow once that exercise has finished.
Answer from the register as it stands, flag clearly that the three fields the board asked about are not held today, and propose a schema change for the next registration cycle.

Run a targeted exercise against the specific question — for each registered system, whether it touches a customer decision, whether output is acted on unreviewed, and who owns it — and make those permanent register fields.

Commission an independent external review of the AI estate so that the board receives an assurance opinion from a third party rather than management's own account of the bank's exposure to the risk raised.

explanation.correct: The board asked three specific questions and there is a month to answer them. Collecting exactly those three attributes across the registered estate is a bounded exercise that fits the window, and it produces the answer rather than an explanation of why there is no answer. Making them permanent fields is the part that stops this recurring: the board's question is not exotic, it will be asked again, and a register that cannot say whether a system is customer-facing or who owns it will fail the next question too. The gap the board has exposed is in the schema, and the schema change costs nothing to make alongside the collection.

distractors.A: A full re-registration is a larger programme than the question requires and will not complete inside a month. Telling the board that the answer depends on a multi-month exercise reads as an inability to describe the bank's own estate, which is close to the concern that prompted the question.
distractors.B: Reporting the gap honestly is necessary but insufficient. The board asked what the exposure is, and a reply that the register does not hold those fields answers a question about the register instead — while a targeted collection could have produced the real answer in the same period.
distractors.D: External assurance has value once management can describe the estate, and the board has not asked for an opinion on management's account. Commissioning one first outsources a question the CRO should be able to answer and would take longer than the month available.

explanation.concept: When a board question exposes a missing inventory field, answer the question with a targeted collection and add the field permanently in the same exercise. Fixing the schema without answering is evasion; answering without fixing it guarantees the same scramble next time.
explanation.tip: Note the deadline the stem gives you. Options that require a programme longer than the window are excluded on feasibility before you assess whether they are otherwise good ideas.
